$comment: Ground truth for fixture `derive-in-render`: what a correct attribution must
say about the frames this app produces. The accuracy suite reads this file;
it is the fixture's contract, not documentation of it.
`expectedSourceText` exists so the ground truth validates itself. Line
numbers drift the moment someone edits the component, and a stale line number
fails as a wrong attribution rather than as a broken fixture. A test asserts
that each recorded line still contains the recorded text before it asserts
anything about the tool's output.
title: Expensive derive in a render body

bug.summary: OrderTable filters and sorts 10,000 orders in its render body on every keystroke, comparing with localeCompare.
bug.whyItIsRealistic: Each decision is defensible alone: derive instead of caching a stale value, sort by the column the table is sorted by, and use localeCompare because `<` orders diacritics wrongly. Only the combination is slow.

interaction.description: Type a single character into the customer filter.

reproduction.note: Every millisecond figure derived from this fixture must be quoted with these two settings. Unthrottled dev-mode numbers on an M-series Mac are not the user's experience, and throttled numbers are not a benchmark.

culpritLines.role: the derive itself: recomputed on every render because nothing caches it
10,000 lowercasing allocations per keystroke; the smaller half of the cost
the dominant cost, and where sampled stacks are expected to land

acceptableAttribution.note: Any of the three lines counts as correct: they are one expression split across three lines by the formatter, and which one a sampled frame reports depends on whether the sample landed in the comparator or in the enclosing render. Naming App, the input's onChange, or a React internal is wrong.

notAtFault.note: App owns the query state and re-renders on every keystroke, so it is on the stack for the whole frame and is the most likely wrong answer. Blaming it is the specific failure mode this fixture tests for.

$comment: Measured over three consecutive runs under the `reproduction` settings above,
on Chromium 159.0.8154.6 on Apple silicon. Arrays are in run order. Present so
the accuracy suite can assert the fixture still janks, and so a change in these
numbers is visible rather than silently absorbed. They are not a benchmark: see
findings.md on discarding the first run of a session, which behaved completely
differently.
`appRenderMs` is here because App rendered for longer than OrderTable in every
run and React gave it no performance.measure in any of them - it owns the state
the keystroke updates, which is the shape React's span gate excludes. A tool
that reads only the spans will miss the larger of these two components.

$comment: This fixture sits close enough to LoAF's 50ms reporting threshold that most
of its janky interactions produce no entry at all. A suite that asserts one
frame per interaction will be flaky; it must drive many presses and assert
over the aggregate.
Measured over 24 presses under the settings above: development produced 24
React commits of 42-58ms each but only 14-15 long frames, run to run.
Production produced 24 commits and only 6 long frames, with durations
clustered at 50.0, 50.0, 50.2 and 51.0 - so 18 of 24 interactions that
burned around 45ms of main thread were invisible to the trigger.
THE COUNTS IN THE PARAGRAPH ABOVE ARE NOT REPEATABLE. Superseded by
longFramesObservedLater below, which explains why; no suite may assert on
either set. They are not wrong - production's 6 came back on the fifth
capture - they are unrepeatable, which is worse for a test and better as a
finding. The commit count and the '18 of 24 were invisible' shape did
reproduce; only the frame counts moved.
Re-measured five times on 2026-11-15, same machine, same Chromium
159.0.8154.6, same 4x throttle, 24 presses each, all within one hour.
Development gave 14, 14, 14, 23 and 14. Production gave 14, then 6 -
so the 6 recorded above DID come back. The count is not wrong, it is
unrepeatable, which is worse for a test and better as a finding.
The fixture has not changed. Its frames sit a few milliseconds either
side of LoAF's fixed 50ms threshold, so whether a given press clears it
depends on how warm the machine is. The consequence is absolute: the
long-frame COUNT is not a property of this fixture and no suite may
assert on it, because it measures where a distribution happens to sit
relative to a constant.
The aggregate line histogram is the stable quantity and is what the
accuracy suite asserts, at a floor of 60%. Shares seen so far: 73% when
findings.md was written, then 76%, 83%, 69% and 93%, with line 36 ranked
first every time. 69% is the lowest; the floor is doing real work.
The arrays below describe the capture currently in corpus/. Per-frame
values live there; this file records the claim, not a transcription.
Aggregate of the deepest OrderTable.tsx frame per in-window sample across a
24-press development replay: 63 samples over 14 long frames. Line 36 is the
declared dominant culprit; 32 is the component declaration, reached when a
sample lands in the sort but not in the comparator; 49 is the row-rendering
map callback, which is real render work rather than the bug.
The top-ranked line fell inside 34-36 in 13 of 14 frames. A single-frame
assertion is not a fair test of line attribution; this is.
